newsitem.title: FRANCE: Iraq buys French wheat with oil revenue.
newsitem.headline: Iraq buys French wheat with oil revenue.

text.p: Iraq bought at least 100,000 tonnes of French wheat on Thursday in one of its first food purchases since resuming oil exports, grain traders said.
It had been negotiating for several days to buy the wheat using money raised through the export of crude under a United Nations humanitarian oil-for-food deal.
Such grain deals are rarely confirmed in public but one European trader said the full amount on its way to Iraq might be as much as 200,000 tonnes, to arrive in January and February.
Such a deal would be worth at least $30 million, traders said, and another $6 million might have to be added for freight and other costs linked to the complex U.N. deal.
Traders said Iraq was thought to have bought the French wheat at the equivalent of $150 per tonne, about half wheat's value eight months ago when prices were at record highs.
But the exact value of the deal was difficult to establish because of unknown factors in the U.N. monitoring process.
Iraq began exporting oil on Monday under a deal to raise money for relief for ordinary Iraqis hit by sanctions imposed after its invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.
France, which has lent conditional support to Iraq's calls for a complete halt to sanctions, is expected to benefit from a range of oil and grain deals.
French oil giants Elf Aquitaine and Total have already signed agreements to buy Iraqi crude under the U.N. scheme.
Iraq is allowed to sell enough oil to raise $2 billion in renewable six-month stages under strict U.N. supervision, while wider economic sanctions will continue to apply.
About half the money raised will be deducted for U.N. costs, reparations and a special relief programme for Kurds in the north.
French grain firms have said initial deals could lead to more purchases to meet Iraq's needs, which Baghdad estimates at two million tonnes of commodities in all.
Traders said Iraq was also rumoured to be buying wheat from Argentina this week but no deals were confirmed.

The Argentine government said last week it thought exporters had placed 80,000 tonnes of wheat with Iraq, though traders said deals were becoming difficult because rain was making Argentine wheat too expensive.
Iraq's main wheat supplier before August 1990 was Australia, followed by the United States, Canada and France.
Baghdad has said wheat will be at the top of its shopping list. Other goods it needs include rice, sugar, vegetable oils, detergents and soaps.
Total imports of wheat over the next six months could reach 1.2 million tonnes, Trade Minister Mohammed Mehdi Saleh said earlier in December.

Western grain traders say Baghdad is especially interested in wheat because it is cheaper for Iraq to produce the flour it needs locally rather than importing it. Iraq's flour mills are said to have been left relatively intact by the 1991 Gulf war.
